title: The Invention of Vaccines
summary: How an English doctor named Edward Jenner used a mild cow illness to invent the world's first vaccine and begin the fight that eventually wiped out smallpox.
poll: Jenner's vaccine idea was one of the most important inventions in all of human history.

versions.title: A Shot That Keeps Us Safe
versions.text:
See that mark on an arm? It is from a shot. The shot is a vaccine.

Long ago, a sickness spread fast. It was smallpox. It made people sick.

A doctor lived in England. His name was Jenner. He saw some farm women.

The women milked cows. Some got cowpox. It came from cows. It was not bad.

Jenner saw more. Those women did not get smallpox. He had an idea.

Could cowpox stop smallpox? In 1796, he tried it out.

He took fluid from a sore. He gave it to a boy. The boy was James.

James got a bit sick. Then he got well. Smallpox germs came near him.

James did not get sick! The cowpox kept him safe.

Jenner named it a vaccine. The word comes from a word for cow.

It was the first vaccine. Doctors use many vaccines now. They keep us safe.

By 1980, smallpox was gone. It was gone from the whole world.

versions.title: A Shot That Keeps Us Safe
versions.text:
A small mark on an arm can come from a shot. That shot is a vaccine. It is a tool. It stops sickness.

Long ago, a sickness spread fast. It was smallpox. It made many people sick. Doctors did not know how to stop it.

A doctor named Jenner lived in England. He saw that farm women often got a milder sickness. It was called cowpox. They got it from cows.

Jenner saw more. Those women did not get smallpox. He began to think. Could cowpox stop smallpox?

In 1796, Jenner tried his idea. He took fluid from a cowpox sore. He gave some to a boy. The boy was James Phipps.

James grew a bit sick, then felt fine. Weeks later, smallpox germs came near James on purpose. James did not catch smallpox at all. The cowpox had kept him safe.

Jenner called his new method vaccination. The word comes from vacca, an old word for cow. It was the first vaccine in the world.

Because of Jenner's idea, scientists later made vaccines for other sicknesses too. By 1980, smallpox had gone from the whole world.

versions.title: A Shot That Keeps Us Safe
versions.text:
A small mark that a shot leaves on an arm often comes from a vaccine. It is one of the best tools doctors use. It stops sickness before it starts.

Hundreds of years ago, a bad sickness spread through many towns. It was smallpox. It made large numbers of people very sick. Doctors had no real way to stop it.

A doctor named Edward Jenner lived in England. He saw that milkmaids, the women who milked cows each day, often got a much milder sickness. It was called cowpox.

Jenner saw a big clue. Those milkmaids almost never caught smallpox later. This made him think. Could mild cowpox stop the far worse smallpox?

In 1796, Jenner tried out his idea. He took fluid from a cowpox sore. The sore was on a milkmaid's hand. Then he gave a small bit to a boy. The boy was James Phipps.

James grew mildly sick with cowpox, then got better. Weeks later, Jenner put smallpox germs near James. It was just to test him. James never caught smallpox at all. He had stayed safe.

Jenner named his method vaccination. It comes from vacca, an old word for cow. Many people call this test the world's first true vaccine.

Building on Jenner's work, scientists later made vaccines against many other sicknesses. By 1980, health workers everywhere said that smallpox had been wiped out.

versions.title: A Shot That Keeps Us Safe
versions.text:
A tiny mark that a shot leaves on an arm usually comes from a vaccine. It is one of the best tools doctors have ever made. It stops a sickness before it can even spread.

Hundreds of years ago, a bad sickness called smallpox spread fast through towns. It made huge numbers of people very sick. Doctors had no sure way to stop it.

A country doctor named Edward Jenner lived in England in the late 1700s. He saw something odd. Milkmaids were women who milked cows each day. They often caught a much milder sickness called cowpox from the cows.

Jenner saw a clue that felt very big. Those milkmaids almost never later caught smallpox, even when it was spreading nearby. This made him wonder: could mild cowpox guard a person from the far worse smallpox?

In 1796, Jenner chose to test his idea. He took fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. She had just caught cowpox from a cow. Then he gave a small bit to a boy named James Phipps.

James grew mildly ill with cowpox for a short while, then got well again. Weeks later, Jenner put real smallpox germs near James, just to see if the boy was safe. James never got smallpox at all.

Jenner named his method vaccination, taken from vacca, the old Latin word for cow. People now call this careful test the world's very first true vaccine.

Building right on Jenner's find, many scientists later made vaccines against other bad sicknesses. By 1980, health workers across the world said that smallpox had been wiped out for good.

versions.text:

Building on Jenner's find, scientists later made vaccines that protect people against many other sicknesses. By 1980, health workers across the world announced that smallpox had been wiped out for good.

versions.text:
The tiny mark that a shot leaves on an arm usually comes from a vaccine. A vaccine trains the body's immune system to recognize a specific germ. It can then fight that germ off before it ever makes someone truly ill.

Hundreds of years ago, a dangerous and contagious disease called smallpox spread quickly through towns and villages. It made enormous numbers of people seriously ill, and it sometimes proved fatal. Doctors of that era had no dependable way to stop it spreading.

A country doctor named Edward Jenner lived in England in the late 1700s. He noticed something genuinely curious. Milkmaids, the women who milked cows every day, frequently caught a far milder illness called cowpox from the animals they cared for. It rarely troubled them beyond a few small sores.

Jenner noticed a clue that struck him as remarkably significant. Milkmaids who had already had cowpox almost never later caught smallpox. This held true even as the far deadlier disease spread through nearby villages. It made him wonder whether the mild cowpox illness might protect a person against the more dangerous smallpox.

In 1796, Jenner finally resolved to put his theory to a real test. He collected fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. She had recently caught the illness from a cow. Then he gave a small amount of that fluid to a healthy young boy named James Phipps.

James grew mildly ill with cowpox for a short while, then recovered completely within days. Several weeks later, Jenner deliberately exposed James to real smallpox germs. He wanted to see whether the boy had truly been protected. Remarkably, James never developed smallpox at all.

Jenner named his method vaccination, borrowing the term from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Many historians regard this careful experiment as the world's very first true vaccine. It permanently changed how doctors understood and fought infectious disease.

Building directly on Jenner's discovery, later generations of scientists developed vaccines that protect people against countless other dangerous diseases. In 1980, health officials across the globe finally announced that smallpox, once among the deadliest diseases in history, had been completely eliminated.

versions.title: The First Vaccine
versions.text:
The tiny mark that a shot leaves on an arm usually comes from a vaccine. A vaccine trains the body's immune system to recognize a specific germ. It can then fight that germ off before it ever gets the chance to make someone genuinely ill.

Centuries ago, a dangerous and contagious disease called smallpox spread quickly through towns and villages across whole regions. It made enormous numbers of people seriously ill. In many unfortunate cases, it proved fatal. Doctors of that era had no dependable way to prevent its spread.

A country doctor named Edward Jenner practiced medicine in England in the late 1700s. He noticed something that struck him as genuinely curious. Milkmaids, the women responsible for milking cows every day, frequently caught a far milder illness called cowpox from the animals under their care. It seldom troubled them beyond a few small sores.

Jenner identified a clue that struck him as remarkably significant. Milkmaids who had already endured cowpox almost never subsequently caught smallpox. This held true even as the far deadlier disease spread unchecked through surrounding villages. This careful observation led him to wonder whether the mild cowpox illness might somehow protect a person against the far more dangerous smallpox.

In 1796, Jenner finally resolved to put his carefully considered theory to a real scientific test. He collected fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes. She had recently caught the illness from a cow. Then he deliberately gave a small amount of that fluid to a healthy young boy named James Phipps.

James grew mildly ill with cowpox for a short while, then recovered completely within days. Several weeks later, Jenner deliberately exposed James to real smallpox germs. He wanted to determine whether the boy had truly been made immune. Remarkably, James never developed smallpox at all.

Jenner named his method vaccination, deliberately borrowing the term from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Many historians now regard this meticulous experiment as the world's very first true vaccine. It permanently transformed how doctors understood and fought infectious disease.

Building directly on Jenner's pioneering discovery, later generations of scientists developed vaccines capable of protecting people against countless other dangerous diseases, from measles to polio. In 1980, health officials across the globe finally announced that smallpox, once among the deadliest diseases in human history, had been completely eliminated.

versions.title: Jenner and the First Vaccine
versions.text:
The tiny mark a shot leaves on an arm usually comes from a vaccine. A vaccine trains the immune system to recognize a specific pathogen, long before that pathogen has any chance of causing a genuine epidemic.

Centuries ago, a dangerous and contagious disease called smallpox spread relentlessly through towns and villages. It made enormous numbers of people seriously ill, and in many cases, it proved fatal. Physicians of that era had no dependable way to prevent its spread.

Even before Jenner's famous experiment, some physicians practiced a risky technique called inoculation. They deliberately exposed a healthy person to a small amount of real smallpox, hoping for a milder case. The method sometimes worked, but it could also spread the full disease and occasionally killed the patient.

A country doctor named Edward Jenner practiced medicine in England in the late 1700s. He noticed something far safer. Milkmaids who milked cows every day frequently caught a much milder illness called cowpox, and it rarely troubled them beyond a few small sores.

Jenner identified a clue that struck him as remarkably significant. Milkmaids who had endured cowpox almost never later caught smallpox, even as the deadlier disease spread through nearby villages. This observation led him to wonder whether cowpox could confer genuine immunity against smallpox.

In 1796, Jenner finally resolved to test his theory scientifically. He collected fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and introduced a small quantity into a healthy boy named James Phipps. Weeks later, he exposed James to real smallpox, and the boy never developed the disease.

Jenner named his safer method vaccination, borrowing the term from vacca, the Latin word for cow. Many historians regard this experiment as the beginning of modern immunology, since it inspired generations of scientists to design vaccines against countless other pathogens.

In 1980, the World Health Organization formally declared that smallpox had been eradicated worldwide. It is the only human disease ever eliminated entirely through vaccination, a monumental achievement built on Jenner's insight.

versions.title: Jenner and the First Vaccine
versions.text:
The tiny mark that a routine shot leaves on an arm usually comes from a vaccine, a sophisticated medical tool engineered to train the immune system to recognize a specific pathogen well before that pathogen could ever trigger a genuine epidemic among an unprotected population, and this entire branch of medicine traces back to a single, carefully reasoned experiment conducted more than two centuries ago in rural England.

Centuries before that experiment, a dangerous and highly contagious disease known as smallpox spread relentlessly through towns and villages across entire regions of the world, inflicting serious illness upon staggering numbers of people and, in countless tragic instances, proving fatal, while physicians of that distant era possessed no dependable method whatsoever for halting its merciless advance across continents, leaving entire communities vulnerable generation after generation.

Even before Jenner's celebrated experiment, some physicians practiced a considerably riskier technique known as inoculation, in which they deliberately exposed a healthy person to a small amount of actual smallpox in the hope of inducing a comparatively milder case; the method occasionally succeeded, yet it could just as easily spread the full disease and sometimes killed the very patient it was meant to protect, a troubling uncertainty that made many physicians understandably hesitant to rely upon it as a dependable solution.

A country doctor named Edward Jenner, who practiced medicine in rural England during the late 1700s, noticed something considerably safer unfolding among the population he served, since milkmaids who milked cows every day frequently contracted a much milder illness called cowpox that rarely troubled them beyond a handful of small sores on their hands and forearms, a pattern too consistent for Jenner to dismiss as mere coincidence.

Jenner identified a clue that struck him as remarkably significant: milkmaids who had already endured cowpox almost never subsequently caught smallpox, even as the far deadlier disease spread unchecked through surrounding villages, and this careful, patient observation, gathered over years of ordinary medical practice, led him to wonder whether cowpox might confer genuine, lasting immunity against smallpox itself, rather than merely a brief and temporary resistance.

In 1796, Jenner finally resolved to test his theory in a rigorous, scientific fashion, collecting fluid from a cowpox sore on the hand of a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and deliberately introducing a small quantity into a healthy boy named James Phipps; several weeks afterward, he deliberately exposed James to genuine smallpox germs, and remarkably, the boy never developed the disease at all, decisively confirming his careful hypothesis and establishing a method that could be repeated and verified by others.

Jenner named his considerably safer method vaccination, deliberately borrowing the term from vacca, the Latin word for cow, and many historians regard this landmark experiment as the formal beginning of modern immunology, since it directly inspired generations of scientists to design vaccines against countless other dangerous pathogens over the two centuries that followed.

In 1980, the World Health Organization formally declared that smallpox had been eradicated worldwide, making it the only human disease ever fully eliminated through vaccination, a genuinely monumental public health achievement built directly upon Jenner's eighteenth-century insight, persistence, and willingness to test a theory that many of his contemporaries initially dismissed as absurd or even dangerous.

Smallpox was mostly a mild illness in rural towns
Jenner's cowpox test led to the first vaccine
James Phipps later grew up to study farm cows
questions.why: The article centers on how Jenner's experiment with cowpox produced the first vaccine and changed how disease is fought.

wrong.A: The article is not about whether milking was easy.
wrong.B: Smallpox is described as dangerous, not mild.
wrong.D: The article never says James studied cows later in life.

questions.stem: According to the article, what made milkmaids different from most other people?
options: They rarely got sick from any illness at all
They traveled often between distant countries
They often caught cowpox from the cows they milked
They worked for many years as trained doctors
questions.why: The article states milkmaids frequently caught cowpox from the animals they cared for.

wrong.A: The article says they caught cowpox, so they did get a little sick.
wrong.B: No travel is mentioned.
wrong.D: Milkmaids were not doctors.

Another local doctor who lived nearby
Sarah Nelmes, the milkmaid with the sore
James Phipps, a healthy young boy

wrong.A: No queen is mentioned.
wrong.B: He did not give it to another doctor.
wrong.C: Sarah Nelmes was the milkmaid the fluid came from, not who received it.

questions.stem: Why did Jenner expose James to real smallpox germs weeks later?
options: To test whether James was now truly protected
To compare James directly to Sarah Nelmes
To make James sick on purpose for no clear reason
To see whether James still liked and trusted him

wrong.B: He was not comparing James to Sarah at that point.
wrong.C: Jenner had a clear scientific reason, not no reason.
wrong.D: This is not mentioned as a reason.

questions.stem: What can you infer about why many doctors trusted Jenner's method over inoculation with real smallpox?
options: It cost a great deal more money to perform
It took much longer for doctors to carry out
It was actually far more dangerous to try
It was gentler on patients and still worked

wrong.A: Cost is not discussed in the article.
wrong.B: Speed of the method is not discussed.
wrong.C: Cowpox was described as far less dangerous than real smallpox.

questions.stem: In this article, what does the word immune describe?
options: Someone whose body can resist a disease
Someone who studies cows for a living
Someone who is currently very sick

wrong.C: Immune is close to the opposite of being very sick.
wrong.D: Immune has nothing to do with where a person lives.

questions.stem: How is the article mostly organized?
options: As a sequence of events leading to a discovery
As an argument between two rival scientists
As a set of plain instructions for a shot

wrong.B: There is no argument between two scientists in the article.
wrong.C: The article is not written as a set of instructions.
wrong.D: The facts are connected, not a random list.

questions.stem: What happened to smallpox after vaccines spread around the world?
options: It only ever disappeared from England
It gradually changed into a new disease
It became noticeably more common
It was completely wiped out by 1980
questions.why: The article states that by 1980, smallpox had been completely eliminated worldwide.

wrong.A: The elimination was worldwide, not just in England.
wrong.B: The article does not say smallpox changed into a new disease.
wrong.C: The opposite happened; cases dropped to zero.

MID.prompt: Using details from the article, explain how Jenner's observation about milkmaids led to the invention of the vaccine and to the end of smallpox.
checklist: Explains Jenner's observation about milkmaids and cowpox
Describes the test with Sarah Nelmes and James Phipps
Connects the invention to smallpox being wiped out by 1980
MID.modelAnswer: Edward Jenner, an English doctor, noticed that milkmaids who caught the mild illness cowpox almost never caught the much more dangerous disease smallpox. In 1796, he tested this idea by taking fluid from a cowpox sore on a milkmaid named Sarah Nelmes and giving it to a boy named James Phipps. James became mildly ill with cowpox, recovered, and then did not catch smallpox even when exposed to it on purpose. Jenner named his method vaccination, and his discovery eventually led scientists to develop vaccines against many diseases. By 1980, these vaccines had helped wipe smallpox out completely around the world.

keyWords.definition: the body's ability to resist a particular disease, often built up after exposure to it or to a vaccine
keyWords.example: Recovering from the illness gave her lasting immunity to it.

keyWords.definition: to completely get rid of something, especially a disease, everywhere it exists
keyWords.example: Scientists hope to eradicate several more diseases in the coming decades.

keyWords.definition: an older, riskier method of deliberately giving someone a small dose of a real disease to try to produce a milder case
keyWords.example: Inoculation with real smallpox sometimes protected people, but it could also make them seriously ill.

keyWords.definition: a germ, such as a virus or bacterium, that can cause disease
keyWords.example: Doctors worked to identify the exact pathogen causing the outbreak.

keyWords.definition: an outbreak of a disease that spreads quickly to a large number of people in an area
keyWords.example: The city set up extra clinics to respond to the epidemic.

A cowpox observation led Jenner to invent vaccination and helped eradicate smallpox

wrong.C: The article presents inoculation as riskier, not safer, than Jenner's method.

It only ever seemed to work on young children

A detailed report sent by another country's doctors
A random guess made with no real evidence

wrong.A: The article presents Jenner's experiment positively, not critically.
wrong.B: The 1980 declaration is about eradication, not about explaining inoculation.
wrong.C: The declaration shows a vaccine succeeding completely, not failing.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why Jenner's method eventually replaced inoculation?
options: It was first discovered by a far more famous scientist
It achieved similar protection against smallpox with far less risk
It was required by a specific law passed in England
It was simply more entertaining for doctors to perform

wrong.A: Fame is not given as the reason in the article.
wrong.C: No law requiring the method is mentioned.
wrong.D: Entertainment value is never discussed.

questions.stem: In this article, what does the word pathogen most likely refer to?
options: A government health agency or office
A type of vaccine given to patients
A germ that can cause a disease

questions.why: The article uses pathogen to describe the kind of germ a vaccine trains the immune system to recognize.

wrong.B: A vaccine targets a pathogen; it is not the pathogen itself.

questions.stem: How does the article primarily structure its explanation of vaccination's origin?
options: By following a chain of cause and effect to a global result
By listing a series of random facts about England

By comparing several unrelated inventions side by side

wrong.C: The article does not present opposing arguments; it follows one clear development.

questions.stem: Based on the article, which outcome most directly resulted from Jenner's 1796 experiment?
options: Smallpox began spreading faster than it had before
Inoculation became even more popular than before
Milkmaids generally stopped working on farms
The eventual worldwide eradication of smallpox

HIGH.prompt: Analyze how Jenner's 1796 experiment represents a turning point in medical history, using evidence from the article about both the risks of earlier methods and the long-term global outcome.
checklist: Explains the risks of inoculation compared with vaccination
Analyzes the evidence behind Jenner's experiment
Connects the experiment to smallpox's eradication in 1980
HIGH.modelAnswer: Before 1796, the only protection against smallpox was inoculation, deliberately giving someone a small dose of real smallpox, which could itself spread the disease or kill the patient. Edward Jenner noticed that milkmaids who caught the mild illness cowpox almost never later caught smallpox, so he hypothesized that cowpox could produce immunity with far less risk. His experiment on James Phipps confirmed this: the boy developed only a mild illness, then proved resistant to smallpox itself. This discovery, which Jenner called vaccination, launched the field of immunology and inspired vaccines against countless other pathogens. The long-term impact was enormous: in 1980, the World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated worldwide, the only human disease ever fully eliminated, a direct result of the method Jenner first tested on a single farm boy nearly two centuries earlier.

options: They milked cows
They grew crops
They taught school
They sold bread
LOW.why: The text says milkmaids were women who milked cows each day.

wrong.C: Teaching school is not mentioned as their job.
wrong.D: Selling bread is not mentioned as their job.

options: Jenner was born that year
Jenner tested his cowpox idea that year
Smallpox was wiped out that year
James Phipps became a doctor that year
LOW.why: The text says Jenner finally tested his idea in 1796.

wrong.A: Jenner's birth year is not given in the text.
wrong.C: Smallpox was wiped out in 1980, not 1796.
wrong.D: James did not become a doctor in this story.

LOW.stem: What can you tell about cowpox compared to smallpox?
options: Cowpox was much worse than smallpox
Cowpox was much milder than smallpox
They were exactly the same sickness
Cowpox only affected cows, never people
LOW.why: The text shows cowpox barely bothered people while smallpox made many people very sick, so cowpox was milder.

wrong.A: The text shows the opposite is true.
wrong.C: The text treats them as two different sicknesses.
wrong.D: The text says milkmaids caught cowpox too.

LOW.stem: Why is this story a good example of a cause-and-effect pattern?
options: Because Jenner's test caused James to become sick, which led doctors to invent a way to stop smallpox
Because the story lists cow facts in no order
Because the story is only about milkmaids' jobs
Because the story never explains why anything happened

wrong.B: The story is in time order, not a random list.
wrong.C: The story is mainly about Jenner's vaccine idea.
wrong.D: The story explains why Jenner tried his idea and what happened next.

MID.stem: What is the most likely reason the article explains the milkmaids' daily work before describing Jenner's experiment?
options: To show readers how farms operated in general
To set up why milkmaids were the ones who gave Jenner his key clue
To compare farm jobs with being a doctor
To explain why milk is healthy to drink
MID.why: Describing the milkmaids' exposure to cows explains why they, rather than other people, showed Jenner the pattern that led to his idea.

wrong.C: The article does not compare farm jobs to being a doctor.
wrong.D: Milk's healthiness is never discussed.

MID.stem: If a milkmaid in the story had never caught cowpox, what would the article suggest about her risk of smallpox?
options: She would have the same risk as someone who had cowpox
She would likely still be at risk for catching smallpox
She would be completely unable to catch any disease
She would automatically become immune anyway
MID.why: Since cowpox exposure is shown as the reason milkmaids avoided smallpox, someone without that exposure would not have the same protection.

wrong.A: The article shows cowpox exposure made a real difference, so the risk would not be the same.
wrong.C: The article never claims total immunity to every disease.
wrong.D: Immunity is tied to cowpox exposure, not automatic.

MID.stem: How does the structure of the final paragraph support the article's main point?
options: It introduces a brand-new, unrelated topic
It shows the long-term result that grew out of Jenner's original idea
It contradicts everything said earlier in the article
It only repeats the opening sentence word for word
MID.why: The final paragraph connects Jenner's 1796 experiment to the ultimate global outcome in 1980, reinforcing the article's cause-and-effect structure.

wrong.A: The ending stays on the same topic of vaccination's impact.
wrong.C: The ending supports, rather than contradicts, the earlier paragraphs.
wrong.D: The ending adds new information rather than repeating the opening.

MID.stem: Which word from the article is closest in meaning to disease?
options: Vaccine
Sickness
Doctor
Milkmaid
MID.why: Sickness and disease both describe an illness that affects the body.

wrong.A: A vaccine is a tool used against disease, not the disease itself.
wrong.C: A doctor is a person who treats disease, not the disease itself.
wrong.D: A milkmaid is a person, not an illness.

HIGH.stem: Which claim would the article most strongly support with evidence?
options: Inoculation was always safer than relying on natural immunity alone
Jenner's method offered real protection against smallpox with far less risk than inoculation
Milkmaids were the only people ever affected by smallpox
The World Health Organization invented the smallpox vaccine
HIGH.why: The article's evidence, James's protection with only a mild illness, supports the claim that Jenner's method was safer and still effective.

wrong.A: The article presents inoculation as riskier, not uniformly safer.
wrong.C: Smallpox clearly affected far more than milkmaids, as the article implies.
wrong.D: The World Health Organization declared eradication; it did not invent the original vaccine.

HIGH.stem: What is the most likely reason the article contrasts vaccination with inoculation rather than describing vaccination alone?
options: To confuse readers with unrelated information
To help readers understand why Jenner's method was such an improvement
To argue that inoculation should still be used today
To prove that cowpox was more dangerous than smallpox
HIGH.why: Contrasting the two methods highlights exactly what made Jenner's approach a genuine advance in safety and reliability.

wrong.A: The contrast is directly relevant, not confusing or unrelated.
wrong.C: The article presents inoculation as outdated and risky, not something to keep using.
wrong.D: The article shows cowpox as far milder than smallpox, not more dangerous.

HIGH.stem: Based on the article, which best explains why smallpox, specifically, became the first disease eradicated through vaccination?
options: It was the least contagious disease known at the time
Vaccination against it began earliest and eventually reached people worldwide
No one else was affected by any other disease
Inoculation alone wiped it out before vaccination existed

wrong.A: The article describes smallpox as highly contagious, not the least contagious.
wrong.C: Other diseases are referenced as later targets of vaccines, so people were affected by other diseases too.
wrong.D: The article credits vaccination, not inoculation alone, with eradicating smallpox.

HIGH.stem: Which word pair from the article are most closely related in meaning?

Pathogen and germ
Inoculation and eradicate
Doctor and pathogen

wrong.C: Inoculation is a method, while eradicate means to wipe out completely; they are not close in meaning.
wrong.D: A doctor is a person, while a pathogen is a disease-causing organism; they are unrelated in meaning.
